database.title: Portal database
database.blurb: Multi-tenant self-service portal. Provider → Tenant hierarchy; every tenant-scoped table carries tenant_id and is protected by row-level security.

conventions: Primary keys are UUID v4 (gen_random_uuid()) except append-only logs, which use BIGSERIAL.
Every tenant-scoped table has a tenant_id column and an RLS policy keyed on app.tenant_id.
Enum-like columns carry a CHECK constraint or use a PostgreSQL ENUM type.
Soft delete uses deleted_at; uniqueness on soft-deleted tables must be partial (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL).

domains.title: Multi-tenancy
domains.blurb: The Provider → Tenant hierarchy every other table hangs off, with per-tenant settings and auth configuration. Each tenant has exactly one settings row and at most one auth config.

domains.title: Authentication & identity
domains.blurb: Who can log in and how: users and their sessions.

domains.title: Permissions (RBAC)
domains.blurb: Roles per tenant, the global permission catalogue, and the two junction tables that tie users → roles → permissions.

domains.title: GitHub integration
domains.blurb: One provider-level GitHub App serves the whole portal; tenants map to it via installations, and webhook deliveries are stored raw per installation.

domains.title: Approvals & audit
domains.blurb: Service requests and deployments that need sign-off, and the append-only audit trail.

cardinality.why: every tenant gets one settings row at creation; there is nothing to configure twice
a tenant signs in through at most one identity provider
people belong to the tenant that invited them; the same email in two tenants is two users
GitHub sends every delivery for one installation; storing them raw per installation is the audit trail

provider.name: provider
description: Top of the hierarchy. One row per hosting provider.

tenant.name: tenant
description: A customer organisation. Everything tenant-scoped hangs off this row.

tenant_settings.name: tenant_settings
description: Per-tenant settings. Intended to be exactly one row per tenant.

role_permission.name: role_permission
description: Correct junction table: composite PK, both sides indexed.

user_role.name: user_role
description: ⚠ FLAW: junction table with no primary key or unique — duplicate links possible.

github_app_config.name: github_app_config
description: Provider-level single-row App config. NOT tenant-scoped.

github_app_installation.name: github_app_installation
description: Per-tenant installation mapping (tenant -> GitHub App installation).

webhook_delivery.name: webhook_delivery
description: Raw webhook deliveries. No tenant_id — tenant is reachable via installation.

approval_request.name: approval_request
description: An approval is for EITHER a service request OR a deployment.

audit_event.name: audit_event
description: Append-only audit trail. actor may be a user or a system job.
Append-only. Never UPDATE or DELETE rows here.

findings.title: Asserted natural key is not enforced
findings.detail: `(tenant_id, installation_id)` is declared to identify a `github_app_installation` row, but nothing enforces it. Retries, double-submits and webhook redeliveries create duplicates.
findings.suggestion: Add a unique constraint (partial if the table is soft-deleted).
findings.fix_sql: ALTER TABLE github_app_installation ADD CONSTRAINT github_app_installation_tenant_id_installation_id_key UNIQUE (tenant_id, installation_id);

findings.title: Monetary value stored as float
findings.detail: `amount` is binary floating point. 0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3; sums drift; reconciliation against the ledger will be off by cents.
findings.suggestion: Use NUMERIC(p, s) or integer minor units.
findings.fix_sql: ALTER TABLE invoice_line ALTER COLUMN amount TYPE numeric(14,2);

findings.title: Tenant table without row-level security
findings.detail: `invoice_line` carries `tenant_id` but RLS is not enabled, so isolation depends entirely on every query remembering the WHERE clause. One forgotten filter is a cross-tenant leak.
findings.suggestion: Enable RLS and add the standard policy.
findings.fix_sql:
ALTER TABLE invoice_line ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY invoice_line_tenant_isolation ON invoice_line USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid);

findings.title: Table is in no domain
findings.detail: Every table must be claimed by a domain in narratives.json, otherwise it silently falls out of the documentation and of any per-domain backup/retention policy.
findings.suggestion: Add it to the right domain's `tables` list, or delete the table if it is dead.

findings.title: Modelled 1:N but intended 1:1
findings.detail: The narrative says each `tenant` has exactly one `tenant_settings`, but `tenant_id` is not UNIQUE, so the database happily stores five. Application code that does `.single()` or `LIMIT 1` will return an arbitrary row.
findings.suggestion: Make the FK column(s) unique — or make it the primary key.
findings.fix_sql: ALTER TABLE tenant_settings ADD CONSTRAINT tenant_settings_tenant_id_key UNIQUE (tenant_id);

findings.title: No primary key
findings.detail: Without a primary key rows are not individually addressable: no safe UPDATE/DELETE of one row, no logical replication, ORMs misbehave, and duplicates are legal.
findings.suggestion: Add a natural composite key or a surrogate id.
findings.fix_sql: ALTER TABLE user_role ADD PRIMARY KEY (...);

findings.title: Junction table allows duplicate links
findings.detail: `user_role` looks like a many-to-many link table but has no unique constraint across (role_id, user_id). The same pair can be inserted twice; every join through it will double-count.
findings.suggestion: Use the FK pair as the primary key (or add a UNIQUE).
findings.fix_sql: ALTER TABLE user_role ADD PRIMARY KEY (role_id, user_id);

findings.title: Asserted natural key is not enforced
findings.detail: `(delivery_guid)` is declared to identify a `webhook_delivery` row, but nothing enforces it. Retries, double-submits and webhook redeliveries create duplicates.
findings.suggestion: Add a unique constraint (partial if the table is soft-deleted).
findings.fix_sql: ALTER TABLE webhook_delivery ADD CONSTRAINT webhook_delivery_delivery_guid_key UNIQUE (delivery_guid);

findings.title: Foreign key without index
findings.detail: PostgreSQL does not index FK columns automatically. Every DELETE/UPDATE on `service_request` must scan `approval_request` to check the constraint, and every join from the parent side is a sequential scan.
findings.suggestion: Add an index on the FK column(s).
findings.fix_sql: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_approval_request_service_request_id ON approval_request(service_request_id);

findings.title: Foreign key without index

findings.fix_sql: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_approval_request_deployment_id ON approval_request(deployment_id);

findings.title: Either/or foreign keys without a CHECK
findings.detail: `approval_request` has several nullable FKs (service_request_id, deployment_id) that look like an exclusive arc — a row should point at exactly one of them. Nothing stops zero or both.
findings.suggestion: Add a CHECK that exactly one is non-null, or restructure with a supertype.
findings.fix_sql: ALTER TABLE approval_request ADD CONSTRAINT approval_request_one_target CHECK ((service_request_id IS NOT NULL)::int + (deployment_id IS NOT NULL)::int = 1);

findings.title: Enum-like column with no CHECK
findings.detail: `actor_type` is a short string that clearly takes a fixed set of values, but the database accepts anything. Typos become new states, and nobody can list the legal values without reading application code. The comment lists `user | system`, i.e. the values are known.
findings.suggestion: Add a CHECK constraint (cheap, easy to evolve) or a lookup table if values need metadata. Avoid native ENUM types unless the set is truly frozen.
findings.fix_sql: ALTER TABLE audit_event ADD CONSTRAINT audit_event_actor_type_check CHECK (actor_type IN (...));

findings.title: Polymorphic reference without referential integrity
findings.detail: `actor_id` points at different tables depending on `actor_type`. No FK can express that, so orphans accumulate silently and every join needs a CASE. Acceptable for append-only audit data; painful anywhere the target must still exist.
findings.suggestion: Either one nullable FK per target with a CHECK that exactly one is set, or a supertype table that the targets reference.

findings.title: No `tenant_id`; tenant only reachable via 2 join(s)
findings.detail: `sessions` belongs to a tenant only transitively (sessions → users → tenant). Row-level security, per-tenant export/erasure, and per-tenant sharding all need that join. It works at 10 tenants and hurts at 1,000.
findings.suggestion: Denormalise `tenant_id` onto the table (with a composite FK to keep it consistent), or accept the join and write the RLS policy as a subquery now, while it is cheap.

findings.title: Soft delete collides with non-partial UNIQUE
findings.detail: `users` soft-deletes via `deleted_at`, but `(email)` is unique across live AND deleted rows. A user who deletes their account can never sign up again with the same value, and `ON CONFLICT` upserts will resurrect ghosts.
findings.suggestion: Replace with a partial unique index scoped to live rows.
findings.fix_sql: DROP CONSTRAINT/INDEX ...; CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_live ON users(email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

findings.title: Nullable foreign key
findings.detail: `approval_request.approved_by` may be NULL, so the relationship to `users` is optional. That is legitimate (e.g. approved_by before approval) but often a modelling shrug: a row with no owner, or two nullable FKs that are secretly an either/or.
findings.suggestion: Confirm the optionality is a domain rule; document it in the column comment.

findings.title: Tenant FK relies on the default ON DELETE NO ACTION
findings.detail: Deleting a `tenant` row will fail while `audit_event` rows exist. Fine if tenants are never hard-deleted; a surprise the day offboarding/GDPR erasure is built.
findings.suggestion: State the intent explicitly: CASCADE, RESTRICT, or an offboarding job.

findings.title: TIMESTAMP without time zone
findings.detail: `occurred_at` stores wall-clock time with no zone. It reads back differently depending on the session's TimeZone, and DST transitions produce ambiguous values.
findings.suggestion: Use TIMESTAMPTZ.
findings.fix_sql: ALTER TABLE audit_event ALTER COLUMN occurred_at TYPE timestamptz;

findings.title: Nullable foreign key
findings.detail: `github_app_config.created_by` may be NULL, so the relationship to `users` is optional. That is legitimate (e.g. approved_by before approval) but often a modelling shrug: a row with no owner, or two nullable FKs that are secretly an either/or.
findings.suggestion: Confirm the optionality is a domain rule; document it in the column comment.

findings.title: Single-row configuration table
findings.detail: `github_app_config` is documented as holding exactly one row. Nothing enforces that (no unique constraint besides the PK), and the day a second instance is needed (a second GitHub App, a staging vs prod config) every reader that does `SELECT * ... LIMIT 1` becomes wrong.
findings.suggestion: Either enforce one row (CHECK on a constant column with a UNIQUE) or give it a discriminator now (`provider_id`, `environment`) while there is only one row to backfill.
findings.fix_sql:
ALTER TABLE github_app_config ADD COLUMN singleton boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true CHECK (singleton);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX github_app_config_one_row ON github_app_config(singleton);

findings.title: Tenant FK relies on the default ON DELETE NO ACTION
findings.detail: Deleting a `tenant` row will fail while `invoice_line` rows exist. Fine if tenants are never hard-deleted; a surprise the day offboarding/GDPR erasure is built.
findings.suggestion: State the intent explicitly: CASCADE, RESTRICT, or an offboarding job.

findings.title: Isolated table
findings.detail: `legacy_import_staging` references nothing and nothing references it. Either it is a staging/log table (fine, say so), or it is dead, or it is the seed of a second data model growing beside the first.
findings.suggestion: Document its purpose or drop it.

findings.title: Hub table: referenced by 10 tables
findings.detail: Any change to its key, its delete semantics, or its partitioning touches every dependent. Migrations on hub tables need the longest lock windows and the most careful rollout.
findings.suggestion: Treat schema changes here as breaking changes with a written rollout plan.
